prompt.context: The CEO of a major client has requested a short-term study examining a small part of the client's product portfolio. The company has a small division that manufactures automatic drip coffeemakers for the US and Canadian market. The division has been steadily producing coffeemakers for 20 years and has made few changes to the business over its history. The client has always enjoyed healthy margins for the coffeemaker division, and annual volumes have been steady. Recently, however, the coffeemaker division's profits have been declining.
prompt.question: The CEO wants to understand what is going on. What broader insights would you want to explore first to answer the CEO's question?

clarifying_info.q: Have fixed or variable costs changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: The production lines and facilities are mature; the business has been steady and efficient. No major changes to fixed or variable cost inputs have occurred recently.

clarifying_info.q: What is happening with production capacity?
clarifying_info.a: All production occurs at a facility in Michigan. The plant is operating at about 90-95% capacity.
The division produces 4-cup, 10-cup, and 12-cup coffeemakers. The overall mix between these categories has been fairly consistent.

exhibits.title: Number of Coffeemakers Sold (in thousands of units) by Retailer Category
exhibits.shows: A table showing coffeemaker unit sales (thousands) from 2003 to 2010 broken out by individual retailer and retailer category. National Chains include Best Buy, Target, Walgreens, Sears, Office Max, Kohl's, Bed Bath and Beyond, Costco, BJ's, and Walmart. Non-National Retailers include Grocery, Medium Retailers, Smaller Retailers, and Other. Each section shows 4-cup, 10-cup, and 12-cup unit sales and totals per year, with a memo row showing each segment as a percent of total sales.

framework: Market: How are competitors performing? Have new competitors entered? Have new substitutes or technologies emerged? Where are prices relative to competitors?
Customer: Are customer preferences changing? Has product mix shifted? Are customers more or less price sensitive? Have customers become more concentrated?
Channel: How do we reach our customers? Has distribution changed? Are retail outlets changing? Are channels consolidating? How are retail sales prices established?

questions.prompt: Question 1 (Exhibit 1): What conclusions can you make from this data?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify that National Chains are making up an increasing share of the client's sales — rising from ~46% in 2003-2004 to 63% in 2010 — while Non-National Retailers have declined correspondingly. Bonus points for noting that Walmart alone accounts for approximately 25% of total coffeemaker sales (188k out of 782k in 2010), creating significant single-buyer concentration risk.

questions.prompt: Question 2 (Exhibit 1): What are the implications of this shift toward National retailers?
questions.guidance: Larger national chains have more bargaining power and are putting increasing pressure on the division to provide volume-based discounts, squeezing the company's margins. Walmart's outsized share further reduces the client's negotiating leverage.

questions.prompt: Math Test: What percent of the market do you think the client has?
questions.guidance: The candidate must estimate total annual coffeemaker sales in the US and Canada, then divide the client's ~800k unit volume by that figure. Any logical estimation is acceptable. Strong candidates will include non-household locations such as offices and hotels. The final estimate should land in the range of 10-15 million units annually, yielding roughly 5-8% market share, making the client a small player with limited bargaining leverage over retailers.

math.setup: US households ~100 million, Canada ~10 million = ~110 million households. About 65% own electric coffeemakers. Replacement cycle approximately 7 years on average.
steps: Add non-household demand (offices, hotels): ~2-4M additional units
math.answer: The client holds approximately 5-8% market share and is a relatively small player with limited bargaining leverage over retailers.

questions.prompt: Follow-up Question: The CEO mentions that the dishwashers and cooking appliances division recently launched a website to sell its products. He wants to know if a website would also work for coffeemakers. Do you think it will work?
questions.guidance: Any answer is acceptable if the candidate can create a logically structured argument and identifies at least a couple of risks. The candidate should also want to understand the potential profitability of a website. Reasons for a website: captures the margin currently going to retailers; reduces dependency on national chains and could add volume; the company already has existing web capabilities from another division. Reasons against: need to understand economics of fixed costs; coffeemakers are more of an immediate purchase decision than dishwashers or ovens, so customers may not want to wait for shipping; increased competition from sites like Amazon; customers may already purchase the client's coffeemakers through retailers' own websites, creating a risk of retailer retaliation by pulling products from shelves; the coffeemaker division may lack expertise or skills for online marketing, sales, and fulfillment.

questions.prompt: Math Question 2: Given the following information, what percent of the company's sales would the client need to achieve for the website to break even? Annual website costs: $500k; Additional marketing costs: $300k; Average retail price of coffeemaker: $60; Additional $4 per coffeemaker for handling; Customer pays for shipping. (Provide only if asked: margin on coffeemakers is 40%)
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute the per-unit profit on website sales, then derive break-even volume and express it as a percentage of total annual sales. Total annual sales are approximately 800k units.

math.setup: Margin = 40%, so COGS = $60 x 60% = $36. Profit per unit before handling = $60 - $36 = $24. After $4 handling cost, profit per unit through website = $20. Total website annual costs = $500k + $300k = $800k.
math.answer: The website breaks even at 40,000 units, or approximately 5% of the client's annual sales volume of ~800k units.

brainstorming.prompt: The CEO appreciates the work on identifying the national retailer margin squeeze and the website breakeven analysis. He would also like your insight on other possible ideas. What other solutions might you suggest?

categories.name: Corporate Strategy and M&A
ideas: Investigate selling the coffeemaker division to another coffeemaker manufacturer
Investigate purchasing other coffeemaker manufacturers to gain scale and leverage with retailers

categories.name: Production and Cost
ideas: Move production overseas to increase margins

categories.name: Channel and Distribution
ideas: Consider exclusive retailing rights with one distributor
Seek other channels such as Starbucks or hotel chains
Increase focus and attention on small-to-medium retailers to reduce dependency on national chains

categories.name: Marketing and Pricing
ideas: Increase marketing efforts to create a pull-strategy from customers, increasing leverage with retailers
Consider raising prices to offset margin loss, subject to investigation of customer price sensitivity

recommendation: Recommend launching a direct-to-consumer website to capture retailer margins and reduce dependency on national chains; it breaks even at just 5% of current annual volume, making it a low-risk initial investment
Alternatively or in parallel, pursue strategies to improve bargaining leverage such as acquiring other coffeemaker manufacturers or redirecting sales toward small-to-medium retailers
risks: National retailers may retaliate by pulling the client's products from shelves if a direct channel is launched
Online competition from Amazon and other websites may erode website channel economics
Coffeemakers are impulse purchases and customers may be unwilling to wait for online shipping
The coffeemaker division may lack the digital marketing and fulfillment capabilities required to run a successful direct channel
Moving production overseas carries operational, quality, and reputational risk
next_steps: Conduct deeper profitability analysis on the website channel, including sensitivity on conversion rates and marketing spend
Assess retailer contract terms for exclusivity or most-favored-nation clauses that might restrict a direct channel
Evaluate acquisition targets in the coffeemaker space to improve retailer bargaining leverage
Pilot the website at small scale before full rollout to test customer demand and fulfillment costs
